[ASSISTANT] Common symptoms of a potential heart attack include chest pain or discomfort, pain in other areas of the upper body, shortness of breath, sweating, lightheadedness, dizziness, nausea, or vomiting.  
[ASSISTANT] In an emergency, it is crucial to call emergency services immediately (911 in the US) or get the person to the hospital as soon as possible.  
[ASSISTANT] If prescribed by a doctor, the person may need to take an aspirin or nitroglycerin.  
[ASSISTANT] It is important to stay calm and reassure the person, avoiding unnecessary movements or activities.  
[ASSISTANT] The average response time for an ambulance in the US is around 8 minutes, but it can vary based on location and circumstances.  
[ASSISTANT] A heart attack can last from 20 minutes to several hours if left untreated, with longer durations leading to greater damage to the heart muscle.  
[ASSISTANT] To prevent a heart attack, one should eat a heart-healthy diet, exercise regularly, manage stress, quit smoking, limit alcohol intake, control blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood sugar levels, and maintain a healthy weight.  
[ASSISTANT] Risk factors for a heart attack include age (men over 45, women over 55), family history, high blood pressure, high cholesterol levels, diabetes, obesity, and smoking.  
[ASSISTANT] Seemingly healthy individuals can suffer from heart attacks, and undiagnosed heart disease can occur.  
[ASSISTANT] A "silent" heart attack can happen without warning signs or symptoms, and damage to the heart muscle can still occur.  
[ASSISTANT] To prevent silent heart attacks, one should maintain a healthy lifestyle, control risk factors, seek regular medical checkups, and be aware of family history of heart disease.  
[ASSISTANT] There is no foolproof way to predict or prevent a silent heart attack, but managing risk factors can limit chances of experiencing one.
